prompt: Why is a Cook–Levin tableau still polynomial in input length when its machine runs in polynomial time?

options.text: It stores every possible computation in a separate row
options.explanation: Rows describe steps of one candidate run; all candidate runs are represented by different assignments.

options.text: Both grid dimensions are polynomial, with fixed local work per cell
options.explanation: Time bounds the rows and the reachable tape positions; the fixed machine gives constant local constraints.

options.text: SAT always has only polynomially many assignments
options.explanation: A polynomial-size formula may have exponentially many assignments.

options.text: The reduction first finds an accepting computation
options.explanation: The encoding is built without knowing which, if any, choices lead to acceptance.

workedExample: The tableau has one dimension for time and one for tape positions. Each dimension is polynomially bounded, so their product is still polynomial. With a fixed machine, each cell adds only a constant number of local constraints. Exponentially many assignments to those variables do not make the written formula exponentially long.

prompt: Why does the Cook–Levin proof need L to be decided in **polynomial** time by the nondeterministic machine, rather than, say, time 2ⁿ (where n is the input length)?

options.text: Because SAT can only express polynomial-time computations
options.explanation: A formula can describe a computation of any fixed length; the problem is the size of the formula, not expressiveness.

options.text: With time 2ⁿ the tableau, and hence the formula, would have about 4ⁿ cells, so building it would take exponential time and it would no longer be a polynomial-time reduction
options.explanation: Correct. A reduction must run in polynomial time, which bounds the formula's size. The tableau's side length is the running time, so a 2ⁿ-time machine gives a 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ grid.

options.text: Because nondeterministic machines can't run for exponential time
options.explanation: They can; NEXPTIME is exactly the class of problems decided by nondeterministic machines in exponential time.

options.text: It doesn't; the proof works for any time bound
options.explanation: The same encoding exists for any time bound, but only polynomial bounds give polynomial-size formulas, which is what makes it a Karp reduction.

workedExample: Writing the whole tableau requires writing each time-by-tape cell and its local constraints. Squaring a polynomial bound stays polynomial; squaring an exponential bound stays exponential. The encoding still represents a computation, but would fail the polynomial-time requirement for a Karp reduction.
